sents: At some point in history, humans discovered that ice preserved food.
There is evidence that winter ice was stored to preserve food in the summer as far back as 10,000 years ago.
Two thousand years ago, the inhabitants of South America's Andean mountains had a unique means of conserving potatoes for later consumption.
They froze them overnight, then trampled them to squeeze out the moisture, then dried them in the sun.
This preserved their nutritional value – if not their aesthetic appeal.

simp.text: Humans discovered that ice preserved food.
Winter ice was stored 10,000 years ago.
Andean people had a unique means of conserving potatoes
They froze, trampled, then dried them.
This preserved nutritional value.

paras.main: Con người dùng băng bảo quản thức ăn từ rất lâu; người Andes bảo quản khoai tây bằng cách đông lạnh rồi phơi khô.

sents: Natural ice remained the main form of refrigeration until late in the 19th century.
In the early 1800s, ship owners from Boston, USA, had enormous blocks of Arctic ice towed all over the Atlantic for the purpose of food preservation.
In 1851, railroads first began putting blocks of ice in insulated rail cars to send butter from Ogdensburg, New York, to Boston.

simp.text: Natural ice remained the main form until the late 19th century.
Boston ship owners had ice towed across the Atlantic
Railroads put ice in insulated cars to send butter

paras.main: Băng tự nhiên được vận chuyển bằng tàu và tàu hỏa để bảo quản thực phẩm.

sents: Finally, in 1870, Australian inventors found a way to make 'mechanical ice'.
They used a compressor to force a gas – ammonia at first and later Freon – through a condenser.
The compressed gas gave up some of its heat as it moved through the condenser.
Then the gas was released quickly into a low-pressure evaporator coil where it became liquid and cold.
Air was blown over the evaporator coil and then this cooled air passed into an insulated compartment, lowering its temperature to freezing point.

simp.text: Australian inventors made mechanical ice.
They used a compressor to force a gas through a condenser.
The gas lost heat, then became liquid and cold.
Cooled air lowered the compartment to freezing point.

paras.main: Năm 1870 người Úc phát minh ra băng nhân tạo bằng hệ thống nén khí.

sents: Initially, this process was invented to keep Australian beer cool even in hot weather.
But Australian cattlemen were quick to realize that, if they could put this new invention on a ship, they could export meat across the oceans.
In 1880, a shipment of Australian beef and mutton was sent, frozen, to England.
While the food frozen this way was still palatable, there was some deterioration.
During the freezing process, crystals formed within the cells of the food, and when the ice expanded and the cells burst, this spoilt the flavor and texture of the food.

simp.text: It was invented to keep beer cool.
But cattlemen realized they could export meat.
A shipment of beef and mutton was sent to England
While still palatable, there was some deterioration
simp.note: `While A, B`: B là ý chính

simp.text: Crystals burst cells, spoiling flavor and texture

paras.main: Công nghệ làm lạnh cho phép xuất khẩu thịt, nhưng tinh thể băng làm giảm chất lượng.

sents: The modern frozen food industry began with the indigenous Inuit people of Canada.
In 1912, a biology student in Massachusetts, USA, named Clarence Birdseye, ran out of money and went to Labrador in Canada to trap and trade furs.
While he was there, he became fascinated with how the Inuit would quickly freeze fish in the Arctic air.
The fish looked and tasted fresh even months later.

simp.text: The modern industry began with the Inuit.
Birdseye went to Labrador to trap and trade furs.
While there, he became fascinated with how the Inuit froze fish
The fish stayed fresh.

paras.main: Birdseye học được cách đông lạnh nhanh từ người Inuit.

sents: Birdseye returned to the USA in 1917 and began developing mechanical freezers capable of quick-freezing food.
Birdseye methodically kept inventing better freezers and gradually built a business selling frozen fish from Gloucester, Massachusetts.
In 1929, his business was sold and became General Foods, but he stayed with the company as director of research, and his division continued to innovate.

simp.text: He developed freezers for quick-freezing.
He built a business selling frozen fish.
The business became General Foods; he stayed as research director.

paras.main: Birdseye phát triển máy cấp đông và xây dựng doanh nghiệp.

sents: Birdseye was responsible for several key innovations that made the frozen food industry possible.
He developed quick-freezing techniques that reduced the damage that crystals caused, as well as the technique of freezing the product in the package it was to be sold in.
He also introduced the use of cellophane, the first transparent material for food packaging, which allowed consumers to see the quality of the product.
Birdseye products also came in convenient size packages that could be prepared with a minimum of effort.

simp.text: He was responsible for key innovations.
Quick-freezing reduced crystal damage
and packaged freezing.
He introduced cellophane
Convenient packages.

paras.main: Birdseye có các đổi mới then chốt làm nên ngành thực phẩm đông lạnh.

sents: But there were still obstacles.
In the 1930s, few grocery stores could afford to buy freezers for a market that wasn't established yet.
So, Birdseye leased inexpensive freezer cases to them.
He also leased insulated railroad cars so that he could ship his products nationwide.
However, few consumers had freezers large enough or efficient enough to take advantage of the products.

simp.text: But there were still obstacles.
Few stores could afford freezers.
So he leased cases.
He leased railroad cars.
However, few consumers had suitable freezers.

paras.main: Vẫn còn trở ngại: cửa hàng và người tiêu dùng thiếu tủ đông phù hợp.

sents: Sales increased in the early 1940s, when World War II gave a boost to the frozen food industry because tin was being used for munitions.
Canned foods were rationed to save tin for the war effort, while frozen foods were abundant and cheap.
Finally, by the 1950s, refrigerator technology had developed far enough to make these appliances affordable for the average family.
By 1953, 33 million US families owned a refrigerator, and manufacturers were gradually increasing the size of the freezer compartments in them.
1950s families were also looking for convenience at mealtimes, so the moment was right for the arrival of the 'TV Dinner'.
Swanson Foods was a large, nationally recognized producer of canned and frozen poultry.
In 1954, the company adapted some of Birdseye's freezing techniques, and with the help of a clever name and a huge advertising budget, it launched the first 'TV Dinner'.
This consisted of frozen turkey, potatoes and vegetables served in the same segmented aluminum tray that was used by airlines.
The product was an instant success.
Within a year, Swanson had sold 13 million TV dinners.
American consumers couldn't resist the combination of a trusted brand name, a single-serving package and the convenience of a meal that could be ready after only 25 minutes in a hot oven.
By 1959, Americans were spending $2.7 billion annually on frozen foods, and half a billion of that was spent on ready-prepared meals such as the TV Dinner.

simp.text: WWII boosted frozen food because tin went to munitions.
Canned food rationed (→ tin shortage), frozen abundant
By the 1950s refrigerators were affordable.
33 million families owned a refrigerator
Families wanted convenience.
Swanson was a large producer.
It launched the first TV Dinner with a huge advertising budget
Served in the same tray used by airlines
Instant success; sales rose.

paras.conn: ①② nguyên nhân chiến tranh → ③④ tủ lạnh phổ biến → ⑤ nhu cầu tiện lợi → ⑥–⑧ TV Dinner → ⑨–⑫ thành công. Chuỗi: **chiến tranh → công nghệ gia dụng → nhu cầu → sản phẩm → doanh số**.
paras.main: Chiến tranh và tủ lạnh phổ biến tạo điều kiện cho TV Dinner thành công.

sents: Today, the US frozen food industry has a turnover of over $67 billion annually, with $26.6 billion of that sold to consumers for home consumption.
The remaining $40 billion in frozen food sales come through restaurants, cafeterias, hospitals and schools, and that represents a third of the total food service sales.

simp.text: The US industry has a turnover of over $67 billion.
$40 billion through restaurants, etc.

paras.main: Ngành thực phẩm đông lạnh Mỹ hiện rất lớn, chủ yếu qua dịch vụ ăn uống.

groups.instr: Complete the notes below. Choose ONE WORD ONLY from the passage for each answer.

items.q: People conserved the nutritional value of ______ , using a method of freezing then drying.
items.exp:
1. Từ khóa: 2,000 years ago, South America, conserved nutritional value of ___, freezing then drying.
2. Đoạn 1 ③④⑤: người Andes ... conserving **potatoes** ... froze overnight, trampled, dried in the sun.
3. `conserved the nutritional value` = `preserved their nutritional value`; `freezing then drying` = `froze them ... dried`.
4. Đáp án: **potatoes**. Ngữ pháp: cần danh từ.

items.q: ______ was kept cool by ice during transportation in specially adapted trains.
items.exp:
1. Từ khóa: 1851, kept cool by ice, specially adapted trains.
2. Đoạn 2 ③: 1851, railroads put blocks of ice in insulated rail cars to send **butter**.
3. `specially adapted trains` = `insulated rail cars`.
4. Đáp án: **butter**. ⚠️ Không chọn *ice* vì cái được giữ lạnh là butter.

items.q: Two kinds of ______ were the first frozen food shipped to England.
items.exp:
1. Từ khóa: 1880, Australia, two kinds of ___, first frozen food shipped to England.
2. Đoạn 4 ③: 1880, a shipment of Australian **beef and mutton** was sent, frozen, to England.
3. `Two kinds of ___` = `beef and mutton` → khái quát là **meat** (đoạn 4 ② có `export meat`).
4. Đáp án: **meat**.

items.q: ○ quick-freezing methods, so that ______ did not spoil the food.
items.exp:
1. Từ khóa: quick-freezing methods, ___ did not spoil the food.
2. Đoạn 7 ②: quick-freezing techniques that reduced the damage that **crystals** caused. Đoạn 4 ⑤: crystals ... spoilt the flavor and texture.
3. `did not spoil` = `reduced the damage`.
4. Đáp án: **crystals**.

items.q: ○ packaging products with ______ so the product was visible.
items.exp:
1. Từ khóa: packaging with ___ so the product was visible.
2. Đoạn 7 ③: introduced the use of **cellophane**, first transparent material, allowed consumers to see the quality.
3. `visible` = `see`; `transparent`.
4. Đáp án: **cellophane**.

items.q: Frozen food became popular because of a shortage of ______
items.exp:
1. Từ khóa: early 1940s, frozen food popular, shortage of ___.
2. Đoạn 9 ①②: WWII boosted frozen food because **tin** was used for munitions; canned foods rationed to save tin.
3. `shortage` = `rationed to save`.
4. Đáp án: **tin**.

items.q: 1950s, USA ● A large number of homes now had a ______
items.exp:
1. Từ khóa: 1950s, large number of homes had ___.
2. Đoạn 9 ③④: refrigerator technology developed, affordable; by 1953, 33 million families owned a **refrigerator**.
3. `a large number of homes` = `33 million US families`.
4. Đáp án: **refrigerator**. ⚠️ Không chọn *freezer* (freezer chỉ là ngăn trong tủ lạnh).

groups.instr: Do the following statements agree with the information given in Reading Passage 1?

items.q: The ice transportation business made some Boston ship owners very wealthy in the early 1800s.
items.exp:
1. Từ khóa: ice transportation business, Boston ship owners, very wealthy.
2. Đoạn 2 ②: ship owners had ice towed all over the Atlantic.
3. Chỉ nói họ vận chuyển băng, không nói họ giàu lên.
4. Thiếu mắt xích "wealthy" → **NOT GIVEN**.

items.q: A disadvantage of the freezing process invented in Australia was that it affected the taste of food.
items.exp:
1. Từ khóa: disadvantage of Australian freezing process, affected the taste.
2. Đoạn 4 ④⑤: some deterioration; crystals... burst cells, **spoilt the flavor and texture**.
3. `affected the taste` = `spoilt the flavor`.
4. **TRUE**.

items.q: Clarence Birdseye travelled to Labrador in order to learn how the Inuit people froze fish.
items.exp:
1. Từ khóa: Birdseye travelled to Labrador in order to learn how Inuit froze fish.
2. Đoạn 5 ②③: went to Labrador **to trap and trade furs**; while there, became fascinated with how Inuit froze fish.
3. Mục đích đến là buôn lông thú, không phải để học; việc quan tâm đến cách đông lạnh đến sau.
4. Mâu thuẫn → **FALSE**.

items.q: Swanson Foods invested a great deal of money in the promotion of the TV Dinner.
items.exp:
1. Từ khóa: Swanson invested a great deal of money in promotion.
2. Đoạn 9 ⑦: with ... a **huge advertising budget**, launched the first TV Dinner.
3. `a great deal of money in the promotion` = `huge advertising budget`.
4. **TRUE**.
pairs: a great deal of money in the promotion

items.q: Swanson Foods developed a new style of container for the launch of the TV Dinner.
items.exp:
1. Từ khóa: Swanson developed a new style of container.
2. Đoạn 9 ⑧: served in the **same** segmented aluminum tray that was used by airlines.
3. `new style` mâu thuẫn với `the same ... used by airlines`.
4. **FALSE**.

items.q: The US frozen food industry is currently the largest in the world.
items.exp:
1. Từ khóa: US frozen food industry currently the largest in the world.
2. Đoạn 10: turnover over $67 billion, v.v.
3. Không so sánh với nước khác.
4. **NOT GIVEN**.

passages.title: Can the planet's coral reefs be saved?

paras.label: A
sents: Conservationists have put the final touches to a giant artificial reef they have been assembling at the world-renowned Zoological Society of London (London Zoo).
Samples of the planet's most spectacular corals ... have been added to the giant tank along with fish that thrive in their presence.
The reef is in the zoo's new gallery, Tiny Giants, which is dedicated to the minuscule invertebrate creatures that sustain life across the planet.
The coral reef tank and its seven-metre-wide window form the core of the exhibition.
'Coral reefs are the most diverse ecosystems on Earth and we want to show people how wonderful they are,' said Paul Pearce-Kelly ...
'However, we also want to highlight the research and conservation efforts that are now being carried out to try to save them from the threat of global warming.'
They want people to see what is being done to try to save these wonders.

simp.text: London Zoo built a giant artificial reef.
We want to show people how wonderful they are.
However, we also want to highlight research and conservation
They want people to see what is being done.

paras.main: Sở thú London dựng rạn san hô với hai mục tiêu giáo dục (→ Q14 v).

paras.label: B
sents: Corals are composed of tiny animals, known as polyps, with tentacles for capturing small marine creatures in the sea water.

These polyps are transparent but get their brilliant tones ... from algae that live within them, which in turn get protection, while their photosynthesising of the sun's rays provides nutrients for the polyps.
This comfortable symbiotic relationship has led to the growth of coral reefs that cover 0.1% of the planet's ocean bed while providing homes for more than 25% of marine species ...

simp.text: Corals are polyps with tentacles for capturing creatures
Polyps get colours from algae, which get protection
algae provide nutrients.
This symbiotic relationship led to reefs that house 25% of marine species.

paras.main: San hô và tảo cùng có lợi (→ Q15 ii).

paras.label: C
sents: As a result, coral reefs are often described as the 'rainforests of the sea', though the comparison is dismissed by some naturalists, including David Attenborough.
'People say you cannot beat the rainforest,' Attenborough has stated.
'But that is simply not true.
You go there and the first thing you think is: where are the birds?
Where are the animals?
They are hiding in the trees, of course.
No, if you want beauty and wildlife, you want a coral reef.
Put on a mask and stick your head under the water.
The sight is mind-blowing.'

simp.text: Reefs are called rainforests of the sea, though dismissed by some naturalists
simp.note: `though`: ý chính là sự bác bỏ

simp.text: Attenborough: that is simply not true.
In rainforests the animals are hiding.
For beauty and wildlife, you want a reef.

paras.main: Có tranh cãi về cách gọi "rainforests of the sea" (→ Q16 iv).

paras.label: D
sents: Unfortunately, these majestic sights are now under very serious threat, with the most immediate problem coming in the form of thermal stress.
Rising ocean temperatures are triggering bleaching events that strip reefs of their colour and eventually kill them.
And that is just the start.
Other menaces include ocean acidification, sea level increase, pollution by humans, deoxygenation and ocean current changes, while the climate crisis is also increasing habitat destruction.

As a result, vast areas – including massive chunks of Australia's Great Barrier Reef – have already been destroyed, and scientists advise that more than 90% of reefs could be lost by 2050 unless urgent action is taken ...
Pearce-Kelly says that coral reefs have to survive really harsh conditions – wave erosion and other factors.
And 'when things start to go wrong in the oceans, then corals will be the first to react.
And that is exactly what we are seeing now.
Coral reefs are dying and they are telling us that all is not well with our planet.'

simp.text: Reefs are under very serious threat from thermal stress.
Rising temperatures strip reefs of colour
And that is just the start.
Other menaces: pollution by humans, ocean current changes ...
More than 90% could be lost by 2050
Corals are the first to react; they are dying.

paras.main: Rạn san hô đối mặt nhiều mối đe dọa và có thể mất hơn 90% vào năm 2050.

paras.label: E
sents: However, scientists are trying to pinpoint hardy types of coral that could survive our overheated oceans, and some of this research will be carried out at London Zoo.
'Behind our ... coral reef tank we have built laboratories where scientists will be studying coral species,' said Pearce-Kelly.
One aim will be to carry out research on species to find those that can survive best in warm, acidic waters.
Another will be to try to increase coral breeding rates.
'Coral spawn just once a year,' he added.
'However, aquarium-based research has enabled some corals to spawn artificially, which can assist coral reef restoration efforts.
And if this can be extended for all species, we could consider the launching of coral-spawning programmes several times a year.
That would be a big help in restoring blighted reefs.'

simp.text: However, scientists are trying to pinpoint hardy corals
Labs; find those that survive warm, acidic waters.
Increase breeding rates
Spawn artificially; several times a year.
That would help restore reefs.

paras.main: Nghiên cứu tìm san hô chịu nhiệt và tăng sinh sản (→ Q18 iii).

paras.label: F
sents: Research in these fields is being conducted in laboratories around the world, with the London Zoo centre linked to this global network.
Studies carried out in one centre can then be tested in others.
The resulting young coral can then be displayed in the tank in Tiny Giants.

'The crucial point is that the progress we make in making coral better able to survive in a warming world can be shown to the public and encourage them to believe that we can do something to save the planet's reefs,' said Pearce-Kelly.
'Saving our coral reefs is now a critically important ecological goal.'

simp.text: Research is conducted worldwide, linked to London Zoo.
Studies are tested in other centres.
Young coral displayed in the tank.
Progress can encourage the public to believe we can save reefs
Saving reefs is critically important.

paras.main: Tiến bộ được chia sẻ và trưng bày để truyền hy vọng.

sents: When asked 'Should robots be used to colonise other planets?', ... Professor Martin Rees said he believed the solar system would be mapped by robotic craft by the end of the century.
'The next step would be mining of asteroids, enabling fabrication of large structures in space without having to bring all the raw materials from Earth.
I think this is more realistic and benign than the ... "terraforming" of planets.'
He maintains that colonised planets 'should be preserved with a status that is analogous to Antarctica here on Earth.'

simp.text: Rees believed the solar system would be mapped by robotic craft.
Next: mining asteroids.
This is more realistic and benign than terraforming.
Colonised planets should be preserved

paras.main: Rees ủng hộ robot khai thác tiểu hành tinh, phản đối thay đổi hành tinh.

sents: ... engineering Professor Daniel Wolpert replied, 'I don't see a pressing need to colonise other planets unless we can bring [these] resources back to Earth.
The vast majority of Earth is currently inaccessible to us.
Using robots to gather resources nearer to home would seem to be a better use of our robotic tools.'

simp.text: I don't see a pressing need to colonise unless we bring resources back.
Most of Earth is inaccessible.
Using robots nearer to home is a better use

paras.main: Wolpert cho rằng dùng robot gần Trái Đất hợp lý hơn.

sents: Meanwhile, for anthropology Professor Kathleen Richardson, the idea of 'colonisation' of other planets seemed morally dubious:
'I think whether we do something on Earth or on Mars we should always do it in the spirit of a genuine interest in "the Other", not to impose a particular model, but to meet "the Other".'

simp.text: Colonisation seemed morally dubious
We should act with genuine interest, not to impose
simp.note: `not to A, but to B`: B chính

paras.main: Richardson thấy thực dân hóa hành tinh đáng nghi về đạo đức.

sents: In response to the second question, 'How soon will machine intelligence outstrip human intelligence?', Rees mentions robots that are advanced enough to beat humans at chess, but then goes on to say,
'Robots are still limited in their ability to sense their environment: they can't yet recognise and move the pieces on a real chessboard as cleverly as a child can.
Later this century, however, their more advanced successors may relate to their surroundings, and to people, as adeptly as we do.
Moral questions then arise.
Should we feel guilty about exploiting [sophisticated robots]?
Should we fret if they are underemployed, frustrated, or bored?'

simp.text: Rees mentions robots that beat humans at chess, but goes on to say...
Robots are still limited in sensing
Later this century, however, they may relate as adeptly as we do.
Moral questions arise.
Should we feel guilty about exploiting robots?

paras.main: Robot còn hạn chế hiện nay nhưng tương lai đặt ra câu hỏi đạo đức.

sents: Wolpert's response ... was this: 'In a limited sense it already has.
Machines can already navigate, remember and search for items with an ability that far outstrips humans.
However, there is no machine that can identify visual objects or speech with the reliability and flexibility of humans....
Expecting a machine close to the creative intelligence of a human within the next 50 years would be highly ambitious.'

simp.text: In a limited sense it already has.
Machines outstrip humans at some tasks.
However, no machine can identify visual objects or speech as reliably
A machine close to human creative intelligence within 50 years is highly ambitious

paras.main: Máy vượt người ở vài việc nhưng chưa có trí tuệ sáng tạo như người.

sents: Richardson believes that our fear of machines becoming too advanced has more to do with human nature than anything intrinsic to the machines themselves.

In her view, it stems from humans' tendency to personify inanimate objects: we create machines based on representations of ourselves, imagine that machines think and behave as we do, and therefore see them as an autonomous threat.
'One of the consequences of thinking that the problem lies with machines is that we tend to imagine they are greater and more powerful than they really are and subsequently they become so.'

simp.text: Fear has more to do with human nature than the machines.
It stems from humans' tendency to personify inanimate objects
We imagine them greater and more powerful than they are.

paras.main: Nỗi sợ máy móc đến từ xu hướng nhân cách hóa của con người.

sents: This led on to the third question, 'Should we be scared by advances in artificial intelligence?' To this question, Rees replied, 'Those who should be worried are the futurologists who believe in the so-called "singularity".

... And another worry is that we are increasingly dependent on computer networks, and that these could behave like a single "brain" with a mind of its own, and with goals that may be contrary to human welfare.

I think we should ensure that robots remain as no more than "idiot savants" lacking the capacity to outwit us, even though they may greatly surpass us in the ability to calculate and process information.'

simp.text: Those who should be worried are the futurologists.
Another worry: networks could behave like a single brain with a mind of its own
We should ensure robots remain idiot savants

paras.main: Rees lo mạng máy tính có thể tự có "ý chí" và muốn giữ robot ở mức hạn chế.

sents: Wolpert's response was to say that we have already seen the damaging effects of artificial intelligence in the form of computer viruses.
'But in this case,' he says, 'the real intelligence is the malicious designer.
Critically, the benefits of computers outweigh the damage that computer viruses cause.
Similarly, while there may be misuses of robotics in the near future, the benefits that they will bring are likely to outweigh these negative aspects.'

simp.text: We have already seen damaging effects of AI in computer viruses
The real intelligence is the designer.
Benefits outweigh damage.
While there may be misuses, benefits likely outweigh

paras.main: Wolpert thừa nhận tác hại hiện có nhưng lợi ích lớn hơn.

sents: Richardson's response to this question was this: 'We need to ask why fears of artificial intelligence and robots persist; none have in fact risen up and challenged human supremacy.'
She believes that as robots have never shown themselves to be a threat to humans, it seems unlikely that they ever will.
In fact, she went on, 'Not all fear [robots]; many people welcome machine intelligence.'

simp.text: None have risen up and challenged human supremacy
Robots have never shown themselves to be a threat; unlikely they ever will
Many people welcome machine intelligence

paras.main: Richardson cho rằng nỗi sợ robot không có căn cứ, nhiều người còn chào đón.

sents: In answer to the fourth question, 'What can science fiction tell us about robotics?', Rees replied, 'I sometimes advise students that it's better to read first-rate science fiction than second-rate science [...] more stimulating, and perhaps no more likely to be wrong.'

simp.text: Better to read first-rate SF than second-rate science: more stimulating, perhaps no more likely to be wrong

paras.main: Rees cho rằng khoa học viễn tưởng hay có thể đáng tin không kém khoa học tầm thường.

sents: As his response, Wolpert commented, 'Science fiction has often been remarkable at predicting the future.
Science fiction has painted a vivid spectrum of possible futures, from cute and helpful robots to dystopian robotic societies.
Interestingly, almost no science fiction envisages a future without robots.'

simp.text: SF has often been remarkable at predicting the future.
It painted a spectrum of futures.
Almost no SF envisages a future without robots

paras.main: Robot là yếu tố nền tảng trong khoa học viễn tưởng.

sents: Finally, on the question of science fiction, Richardson pointed out that in modern society, people tend to think there is reality on the one hand, and fiction and fantasy on the other.
She then explained that the division did not always exist, and that scientists and technologists made this separation because they wanted to carve out the sphere of their work.
'But the divide is not so clear cut, and that is why the worlds seem to collide at times,' she said.
'In some cases, we need to bring these different understandings together to get a whole perspective.
Perhaps then, we won't be so frightened that something we create as a copy of ourselves will be a [threat] to us.'

simp.text: People think reality and fiction are separate.
The division did not always exist.
But the divide is not so clear cut
We need to bring these understandings together
Then we won't be so frightened.

paras.main: Richardson đề nghị thay đổi cách nhìn: kết hợp thực tế và viễn tưởng.

exercises.q:
**A. Simplify** – tìm [S]–[V]:
1. `While the food frozen this way was still palatable, there was some deterioration.`
2. `Richardson believes that our fear of machines becoming too advanced has more to do with human nature than anything intrinsic to the machines themselves.`
3. `The remaining $40 billion in frozen food sales come through restaurants, cafeterias, hospitals and schools, and that represents a third of the total food service sales.`

**B. Đại từ:** `this` trong `this spoilt the flavor and texture` (P1 đoạn 4⑤); `they` trong `they ever will` (P3 đoạn 9②); `these` trong `these negative aspects` (P3 đoạn 8④) chỉ gì?

**C. Paraphrase:** `palatable` – ? · `deterioration` – ? · `dismissed` – ? · `outstrips` – ?

**D.** Vì sao Q10 (Passage 1) là **FALSE** chứ không phải TRUE?

---
exercises.a:
**A.**
1. [S] there (was) [V] was some deterioration (`While ... palatable` là vế nhường bộ; ý chính ở vế sau).
2. [S] Richardson [V] believes (that) our fear has more to do with human nature than anything intrinsic to the machines.
3. [S] The remaining $40 billion ... sales [V] come through restaurants...; mệnh đề `and that represents a third` là bổ sung.

**B.** `this` = **việc tinh thể đá nở ra làm vỡ tế bào**; `they` = **robot**; `these negative aspects` = **việc lạm dụng robot (misuses of robotics)**.

**C.** `palatable` – `tasty / acceptable`; `deterioration` – `decline in quality`; `dismissed` – `rejected`; `outstrips` – `surpasses`.

**D.** Bài nói Birdseye đến Labrador để buôn lông thú (`to trap and trade furs`); việc quan tâm đến cách đông lạnh cá chỉ xuất hiện khi ông đang ở đó. Câu hỏi nói đến "để học" → mâu thuẫn về mục đích.
